title: Economic Inequality

script.speaker: A
script.text: Global wealth inequality has reached record levels. The richest one percent now own more than half the world's wealth.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a staggering statistic. What are the main drivers of this disparity?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Primarily capital returns outpacing wage growth, inheritance concentrating wealth, and tax structures that favor asset holders.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Some argue this inequality is a natural byproduct of innovation and entrepreneurship.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That argument has merit in isolated cases, but systemic inequality undermines social mobility.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Research shows children's economic outcomes correlate more strongly with parental income than in previous generations.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Which suggests the meritocracy narrative is increasingly disconnected from reality.

script.speaker: B
script.text: What policy interventions do you think would be most effective?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Progressive wealth taxes, strengthened inheritance laws, and substantial investment in public education.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Though implementing such policies faces enormous political resistance from those who benefit from the current system.

questions.stemText: What percentage of wealth does the richest 1% own?
What does research show about children's economic outcomes?
options: They correlate strongly with parental income
questions.answer: They correlate strongly with parental income

questions.stemText: Capital ___ outpaces wage growth as a driver of inequality.

Match driver of inequality to mechanism.

pairs.right: Asset owners gain more than workers

answers.Capital returns: Asset owners gain more than workers

fullScript:

A: Primarily capital returns outpacing wage growth, inheritance concentrating wealth, and tax structures that favor asset holders.
B: Some argue this inequality is a natural byproduct of innovation and entrepreneurship.
A: That argument has merit in isolated cases, but systemic inequality undermines social mobility.
B: Research shows children's economic outcomes correlate more strongly with parental income than in previous generations.
A: Which suggests the meritocracy narrative is increasingly disconnected from reality.
B: What policy interventions do you think would be most effective?
A: Progressive wealth taxes, strengthened inheritance laws, and substantial investment in public education.
B: Though implementing such policies faces enormous political resistance from those who benefit from the current system.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work

script.speaker: A
script.text: Automation is projected to displace up to forty percent of current jobs by 2035. How should society respond?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The narrative around automation is often too pessimistic. History shows new technologies create new categories of work.

script.speaker: A
script.text: But the pace of this transition is unprecedented. Previous industrial revolutions occurred over decades.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a valid concern. Workers in their forties and fifties will struggle to retrain for entirely new industries.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Which is why some economists advocate for a universal basic income as a buffer.

script.speaker: B
script.text: UBI has been piloted in Finland and Canada with mixed results. Recipients reported better mental health but labor participation effects were ambiguous.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What about sector-specific retraining programs?

script.speaker: B
script.text: More targeted and potentially more effective. Singapore's SkillsFuture program is often cited as a successful model.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Ultimately, the question is whether we can redistribute the productivity gains from automation more equitably.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Precisely. The technology isn't the problem — it's the distribution of its benefits.

questions.stemText: What percentage of jobs may be displaced by 2035?
Which country's retraining program is cited as a model?
UBI stands for Universal Basic ___.
The real issue is the ___ of automation's benefits.
Match country to automation policy.

A: Which is why some economists advocate for a universal basic income as a buffer.

B: More targeted and potentially more effective. Singapore's SkillsFuture program is often cited as a successful model.

title: Cultural Heritage and Preservation

script.speaker: A
script.text: Should contested colonial-era artifacts be returned to their countries of origin?

script.speaker: B
script.text: This is one of the most charged debates in the museum world. There are legitimate arguments on both sides.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Advocates for repatriation argue these objects were taken under coercive or illegal circumstances.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And that they hold profound cultural and spiritual significance that cannot be replicated by copies.

script.speaker: A
script.text: However, major institutions argue they provide global accessibility and expert conservation.

script.speaker: B
script.text: A somewhat paternalistic position, particularly when the country of origin has developed excellent museums.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Germany has recently begun returning Benin Bronzes. Is this a turning point?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Potentially. Though the British Museum still resists returning the Elgin Marbles to Greece.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What's the ideal resolution?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Collaborative agreements — shared stewardship, rotating loans — rather than absolute ownership.

questions.stemText: What term describes returning artifacts to their origin country?
Which country is returning Benin Bronzes?
The Elgin Marbles are disputed between Britain and ___.
One proposed solution is shared ___ of artifacts.
Match argument to position.

A: Should contested colonial-era artifacts be returned to their countries of origin?
B: This is one of the most charged debates in the museum world. There are legitimate arguments on both sides.
A: Advocates for repatriation argue these objects were taken under coercive or illegal circumstances.
B: And that they hold profound cultural and spiritual significance that cannot be replicated by copies.
A: However, major institutions argue they provide global accessibility and expert conservation.
B: A somewhat paternalistic position, particularly when the country of origin has developed excellent museums.
A: Germany has recently begun returning Benin Bronzes. Is this a turning point?
B: Potentially. Though the British Museum still resists returning the Elgin Marbles to Greece.
A: What's the ideal resolution?
B: Collaborative agreements — shared stewardship, rotating loans — rather than absolute ownership.

title: Mental Health in the Workplace

script.speaker: A
script.text: Burnout has been classified as an occupational phenomenon by the World Health Organization. What's driving it?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The always-on digital culture. The boundary between professional and personal time has almost completely eroded.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Some would argue that flexibility is the trade-off for that connectivity.

script.speaker: B
script.text: In theory. But research shows that when managers send emails at ten PM, employees feel implicitly pressured to respond.

script.speaker: A
script.text: France introduced the right to disconnect legislation. Has it been effective?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Mixed outcomes. The law exists but cultural change is slower than legislative change.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What concrete steps can organizations take beyond policy?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Normalizing conversations about mental health, providing access to counseling, and modeling healthy behavior at leadership level.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Is there a business case for investing in employee wellbeing?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Absolutely. Mental health issues cost the global economy one trillion dollars per year in lost productivity.

The boundary between professional and ___ time has eroded.
Match solution to type.

B: The always-on digital culture. The boundary between professional and personal time has almost completely eroded.
A: Some would argue that flexibility is the trade-off for that connectivity.

B: Mixed outcomes. The law exists but cultural change is slower than legislative change.
A: What concrete steps can organizations take beyond policy?
B: Normalizing conversations about mental health, providing access to counseling, and modeling healthy behavior at leadership level.
A: Is there a business case for investing in employee wellbeing?
B: Absolutely. Mental health issues cost the global economy one trillion dollars per year in lost productivity.

title: Sustainable Cities

script.speaker: A
script.text: By 2050, two-thirds of the world's population will live in cities. How do we make urban environments sustainable?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The most progressive cities are redesigning themselves around people rather than cars.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Copenhagen is often cited as a model. What have they done differently?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Invested massively in cycling infrastructure, district heating systems, and set a target to be carbon neutral by 2025.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What about cities in the developing world, which lack Copenhagen's resources?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Curitiba in Brazil is a fascinating case — achieved excellent public transport on a fraction of European budgets.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What role does urban density play?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Paradoxically, dense cities often have lower per-capita emissions than sprawling suburbs because of shared infrastructure.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So the key is integrated planning — transport, housing, green space together?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Exactly. Cities that plan these systems in isolation inevitably create more problems than they solve.

Which city achieved good transport on a limited budget?
Copenhagen aims to be carbon ___ by 2025.
Dense cities often have lower per-capita ___ than suburbs.
Match city to innovation.

pairs.right: Efficient public transport on low budget

answers.Curitiba: Efficient public transport on low budget

title: The Future of Education

script.speaker: A
script.text: Traditional universities are facing an existential challenge from online learning platforms. Do you think degrees will remain relevant?

script.speaker: B
script.text: For certain fields, yes — medicine, law, engineering. But for many knowledge-based careers, probably not.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What value does a traditional university still provide that online platforms cannot?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The social and networking dimension. The relationships formed during university often matter more than the curriculum.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Some argue universities are gatekeepers that perpetuate privilege rather than enable social mobility.

script.speaker: B
script.text: There's truth in that. Elite universities recruit disproportionately from wealthy backgrounds.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Could microcredentials and portfolio-based hiring replace degrees?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Companies like Google and Apple have already dropped degree requirements for many roles.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So employers are ahead of educational institutions in adapting?

script.speaker: B
script.text: In some sectors. The challenge is that cultural attitudes toward degrees change much more slowly than hiring practices.

options: Dropped degree requirements for many roles
questions.answer: Dropped degree requirements for many roles

Match university benefit to type.

title: Global Migration and Identity

script.speaker: A
script.text: Immigration is one of the most divisive political issues of our era. Why does it provoke such strong reactions?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Because it touches on deeply personal questions of identity, belonging, and economic security simultaneously.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The economic evidence largely shows immigration benefits host economies. Why doesn't that shift public opinion?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Because economic anxiety is real even when aggregate statistics are positive. The gains are distributed unequally.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What about the cultural dimension — concerns about social cohesion?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Research shows that diverse societies with strong integration programs have excellent social cohesion over time.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Canada is often cited as a model for managed immigration.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, their points-based system and multiculturalism policy have created a relatively cohesive diverse society.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What's your view on the ethics of restrictive immigration policies?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Philosophical frameworks differ widely. Cosmopolitans would argue birthplace is a morally arbitrary barrier to opportunity.

Match country/approach to description.

title: Media Literacy in the Digital Age

script.speaker: A
script.text: The term 'post-truth' was Oxford's word of the year in 2016. Are we genuinely in a post-truth era?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The mechanisms for spreading misinformation have become extraordinarily powerful, but humans have always been susceptible to motivated reasoning.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What's different now is the algorithmic amplification of emotionally engaging content regardless of accuracy.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Exactly. Platforms optimize for engagement, and outrage is more engaging than nuance.

script.speaker: A
script.text: How do we rebuild epistemic trust?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Multiple approaches — platform regulation, media literacy education, and supporting quality journalism financially.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Finland has embedded media literacy into the school curriculum from primary level.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And they consistently score among the lowest for susceptibility to misinformation in European surveys.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Is there a tension between free speech and regulating disinformation?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Inevitably. But most liberal democracies already accept limits on speech that causes direct harm.

title: Work-Life Balance in Modern Society

script.speaker: A
script.text: Several countries are trialing four-day working weeks. What does the evidence show?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The most comprehensive trials, in Iceland and subsequently across multiple sectors in the UK, showed maintained or improved productivity.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And the wellbeing outcomes?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Significant improvements in stress levels, sleep quality, and job satisfaction across the board.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Why haven't more organizations adopted it if the evidence is so positive?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Cultural inertia and the assumption that presence equals productivity — particularly resistant in senior leadership.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What about industries where physical presence is non-negotiable — hospitality, healthcare?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The model looks different there — compressed hours, rotating rosters — but the principles can still apply.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Is work-life balance ultimately a personal responsibility or a structural one?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Both, but systemic structures set the parameters within which individual choices are possible.

The assumption is that ___ equals productivity.
Match wellbeing outcome to improvement.

title: Bioethics and Medical Technology

script.speaker: A
script.text: Gene editing technology like CRISPR raises profound ethical questions. Where do you stand?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The therapeutic applications for hereditary diseases are genuinely exciting. Sickle cell disease may soon be curable.

script.speaker: A
script.text: But the line between treatment and enhancement is blurry. If we can edit out disease, why not edit in advantage?

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's the slippery slope concern. Designer babies would fundamentally alter what it means to be human.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And create new forms of inequality — genetic advantages accessible only to the wealthy.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Exactly. The technology itself is neutral, but deployment in an unequal society produces deeply unequal outcomes.

script.speaker: A
script.text: How should this be regulated internationally?

script.speaker: B
script.text: A global treaty similar to the nuclear non-proliferation framework, though getting all nations to sign would be extremely challenging.

script.speaker: A
script.text: China's creation of gene-edited babies in 2018 demonstrated the urgency.

script.speaker: B
script.text: A watershed moment that shocked the scientific community and accelerated calls for international governance.
